analysis.one_liner: Removes the overtime pay exemption that leaves most truck drivers without time-and-a-half pay.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in March 2025 and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has had no further action for the rest of the year.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1938 law exempts many truck drivers from the federal rule requiring overtime pay — time and a half — for hours worked beyond 40 a week. This bill would strike that exemption from the Fair Labor Standards Act, so truckers whose employers fall under federal labor law would earn overtime like most other hourly workers. It was introduced by Senator Padilla with five other senators and referred to the Senate labor committee, which has not taken it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Long-haul and local truck drivers who work long hours but are paid straight time after 40 hours a week. They would gain time-and-a-half pay for overtime hours, worth thousands of dollars a year for drivers who routinely work 60-hour weeks.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the provision that has exempted motor carrier employees from federal overtime pay requirements since 1938.
With the exemption gone, covered truck drivers would be entitled to 1.5 times their regular pay for hours worked beyond 40 a week, the same standard that applies to most hourly workers.
Truckers are among the most overtime-exposed workers in the country; the exemption means employers can schedule long weeks without any premium pay, which shifts the cost of long hours onto drivers.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and motor carriers, which would pay overtime premiums for hours beyond 40 a week. Some of that cost could reach shippers and consumers through freight rates, and some drivers who prefer long single-shift schedules could see employers restructure routes.

drawbacks.text: Trucking companies say the change would raise freight costs and could push some smaller carriers out of an already thin-margin industry, costs that could partly pass through to prices.
Drivers compensated on trip or mileage pay gain less than hourly drivers, and employers could adjust pay rates or schedules in ways that blunt the benefit for some drivers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to drivers is direct and large: time-and-a-half after 40 hours in a profession built on long weeks. The main cost is higher labor expenses for carriers in a competitive, low-margin freight market, some of which would pass to shippers and consumers. The tradeoff favors drivers, and the bill is a single-sentence repeal with no transition provisions, which is simple but offers carriers no phase-in.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate's labor committee, which has not scheduled any action on it, so for now it goes nowhere.

narrative.text: Senator Padilla introduced the bill on March 6, 2025, joined by five other senators: Markey, Sanders, Blumenthal, Warren, and Wyden.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it has remained with no markup, no vote, and no floor action since.
All six sponsors are Democrats or independents aligned with Democrats; no Republican has joined.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies keep paying straight time for overtime hours, and the six sponsors' proposal sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Carriers paying no overtime, so far

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the motor carrier overtime exemption and referred it to the labor committee.

for.name: Sens. Markey, Sanders, Blumenthal, Warren, and Wyden
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — since March 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors are Democrats or the independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no Republican has cosponsored; no vote has occurred to show how the chambers would split.

industries.note: The bill ends their exemption from federal overtime rules, so they would owe time-and-a-half pay after 40 hours a week. Their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against drivers' paychecks.

industries.industry: Freight shippers and retailers reliant on trucking
industries.note: They would likely face somewhat higher freight rates as carriers pass through overtime costs, though a healthier, better-paid driver workforce could reduce the chronic driver shortage and turnover they pay for.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the Senate HELP Committee that get no hearing or markup in their first months almost never advance, and with Republicans holding the Senate majority and no Republican cosponsor, this bill is very unlikely to reach the floor this Congress. Its realistic best path is being folded into a larger labor or appropriations package, which is rare.
